chats.title: how does the memory bench work

messages.text: how does the memory bench work

Every memory system gets the same questions, the same answering agent and the same grader. Only the memory differs.

- **Memory built first.** Each system reads the whole haystack (the chat history or event stream) the way it normally would and builds its store. Tophat starts from an empty store for every question, and the live store is never opened.
- **One answering agent for everyone.** The same model and the same loop (up to 8 tool calls: search, plus read where the system has it), then an answer. So a better score reflects better memory, not a better prompt or a bigger model.
- **One grader.** A separate model labels each answer right or wrong. On LongMemEval it uses the benchmark's official judge prompts, copied verbatim.
- **A ceiling to compare against.** "All in context" puts the whole haystack in the prompt, with no memory system at all. It shows what the answering model can do when nothing is lost.

There are two sets of questions. **2a** is the 15 hardest questions in LongMemEval-S, a public benchmark with about 115k tokens of chat history per question. The questions were chosen before any system ran: the ones published systems most often miss, spread across all seven question types. **2b** is 99 questions about one person's real messages, workouts, sleep and code history, buried in 7,326 events (about 300k tokens).
why should i trust the numbers

Mostly because the comparison is controlled and everything about it is on disk:

- **The questions were fixed in advance** by a seeded rule over other people's published results, not picked after seeing how tophat did.
- **Answer, model and grader are held fixed**, so systems can't win on prompting. The official judge prompts are used where they exist.
- **No leaks.** Tool results never show which sessions hold the answer, and each question gets a fresh store.
- **Every row is kept:** the answer, the judge's label, the full tool trace and the cost per question. Every harness bug found along the way is logged with what was re-run.
- **Other systems run on their own defaults** (Mem0, Zep/Graphiti, Letta, agentmemory, Supermemory), and any deviation, such as local embeddings where the default needs an OpenAI key, is written next to the result.

Where it is weaker:

- **Small n.** 2a has 15 questions, so one question is about 7 points. Treat differences of one or two questions as noise; reruns of the same system moved by one.
- **2b is our own set**, written by us about one person. Read it as a regression test, not an independent ranking.
- **The grader is a model** and occasionally misjudges, mostly on preference questions and disputed answers.
- **Tophat's embedding search was off for every run**, so these are full-text-search numbers.
how does sharing work

Short version: a scope is a group that controls who can read a row. The hub holds only ciphertext and routing metadata, and a note reaches someone when it is written into or shared to a scope they belong to and both sides sync. I'll check the repo notes to confirm the details.

**Scopes and groups.** A scope is a group that controls who can read a row. Every note, entity and work item carries the scopes allowed to read it, and you can read a row if any of its scopes is one of yours. Members have a role in a scope: read, write or admin. Anything you write without naming a scope stays in your private scope.

**What the hub can see.** The hub only relays ciphertext. It stores the sealed log plus routing metadata: device and user ids, group ids and memberships. It never holds a scope key, so it cannot read notes, search them or build pages. It is append-only, with no delete route. The caveat is trust in the operator: whoever runs the hub issues device tokens, so if that matters, run your own hub.

**How a note reaches someone.**
1. You write the note into a scope, or widen an existing one with `tophat-linknotes share note <id> alex,<scope>`.
2. The note is sealed with a fresh key, and that key is wrapped to each scope key allowed to read it.
3. Your next `sync` pushes the ciphertext to the hub.
4. The other person's replica syncs, receives the scope's key for its device and sees the note.

To take it back, run `tophat-linknotes retract note <id>`. The log keeps the record, but replicas hide it.

**Joining a shared scope.** The hub operator gives you a device token. You `init` with it and `sync` to register your device key. The scope's admin runs `scope add <scope> <user> write` and syncs, then you sync again to receive the rows.

shld i switch to dumbbell bench? smt smt stability

Probably yes, but which goal goes first is your call. Here is what I'm going on.

**Your barbell bench, Day A, from your hevy log:**

| day | working sets |
|---|---|
| Oct 20 | 5 at 90 lb, then 5 and 5 at 85 |
| Oct 24 | 5 at 90, then 6 and 6 at 85 |
| Oct 30 | 3 sets of 5 at 90 ("full 90s!") |
| Nov 5 | 6, 5, 4 at 90 |

**Your goals:** you told your friend J on Nov 5 that benching your own weight is "almost there", and on Nov 10 you said the bigger goal is physical ability, being able to frolic, and staying uninjured for a long time.

**Stability:** it comes up in your notes more than once. You wrote "we need stabs lol" on Sep 27, asked on Oct 20 (leg curl) whether your left leg is stronger than your right, and on Nov 5 wrote that you need to work on knee stability at the bottom of the squat. Your left side is the weaker one.

So I think yes, for the longer goal. Dumbbells give each arm its own path, so the weak side can't hide behind the strong one. That is useful, because once the gap shows up you can train it.

The cost is the other goal. You'd leave a barbell progression that is moving right now, and dumbbell bench usually lands around 35 to 40% of the barbell weight per hand (s: recall), so roughly 30 to 35 lb each. If the bodyweight bench is a few jumps away, I'd finish that first and switch the slot after. If you'd rather start finding the left-right gap now, switch now and don't feel bad about the number dropping.

You also said you aren't adding sets. A swap is one for one, so nothing else in the day changes.
ok which one would u do

Hit the bench goal first. You're at 6, 5, 4 at 90, and the last time you got a clean 3x5 at 90 was Oct 30, so the bodyweight bench is probably a few jumps away. Then swap the barbell bench for dumbbell bench in the same slot and start around 30 lb per hand for 3 sets of 8.

If a session ever feels sketchy on the bar before then (you wrote about a shaky third set on Sep 19), that's the day to swap early.
how do i work up to a pistol squat

You're already partway, so here is where your log puts you.

**What you've done (hevy):** on Oct 24 you did 3x8 pistols to a stack of blocks, with a note to start high, do touch-down squats, sweep the free leg forward at the end, then lower the blocks. On Nov 5 it was 2x6 and then 3 reps. If you lowered the blocks that week, a drop in reps is expected; the log doesn't say.

**What's limiting you:** probably not strength. You squatted 6, 6, 7 at 145 lb the same day. Your own notes name the limit: knee stability, range of motion and holding at the bottom on Nov 5, and "hold at bottom to stabilize" on Oct 24. Your left leg is also the one you've flagged as weaker, on the leg curl and the split squats.

**So I'd do this:**
1. **Keep the block progression.** Lower the stack only when every set is clean, as you already planned.
2. **Pause at the bottom.** Two to three seconds, every rep, on the blocks. That is the stability work.
3. **Left leg first.** Do the weaker side first and match the right to its reps.
4. **Eccentric negatives** once the blocks are low: lower for 3 to 5 seconds, then stand up with both legs.
5. **A light counterweight** (5 to 10 lb held out in front) makes the last steps easier. Drop it when the free pistol is close.
6. **Ankles.** If your heel lifts at the bottom, put a small plate under it for now, and work the wall knee-over-toe drill before the set.

Keep it to the slot you already have on Day A; 2 or 3 sets of 3 to 5 per leg is enough.
random but how do people actually figure out what their values are

Researchers use a few methods, and they work better than just thinking about it:

- **Card sorts.** You get a deck of 50 to 100 values (honesty, adventure, security, and so on) and sort them into very important, important and not important. The forced ranking is the point: it is easy to say everything matters, and hard to keep it up when only ten cards fit in the top pile.
- **Questionnaires.** Shalom Schwartz's work, tested across many countries, groups values into about ten broad types, such as achievement, benevolence, security and self-direction, and shows which ones tend to pull against each other.
- **Looking at behaviour.** What you spend your time and money on, and what you are angry about, show your values more reliably than what you say. A gap between the two is the interesting part.
- **Peak and low moments.** Write down the best and worst weeks of the last year and ask what was present or missing.

A practical way to start: do a card sort once, then check it against your calendar and bank statement for a week. Where they disagree, either the values or the schedule needs to change.
is the card sort worth doing alone?

Yes, it takes about 20 minutes and works fine alone. It works better if you do it twice, a week apart, and then look at which cards moved. The ones that stayed in the top pile both times are the ones to trust.

chats.title: encyclopedia cave, what was that place

messages.text: my friend brought me to encyclopedia cave that was crazy what was that place so cool

That's Encyclopedia Cave, the hidden cave near the Stanford Dish. You went on the night of Tue Dec 12, 2023 (s: message): your friend had the group meet at the Dish parking lot around 10:10 pm and at the cave itself around 10:20, and said "Today is for stars". At 1:47 am you texted "Thanks for the great night!" You still have the people from that trip saved together in your contacts under one label.

What it is, from public sources (s: web): a Stanford-hosted photo gallery called "Encyclopedia Cave" (web.stanford.edu/~siegelr/stanford/encyclopediacave.html) from three visits across two years. The captions mention a library, equations, studying in caves, a copy of Origin of Species and a line from Lovecraft left in the cave, so it reads like a study spot people stock with books and notes. A 2023 r/stanford post says the rumor is a cave "somewhere on the dish near the quarry" and that the poster's group couldn't find it.

I couldn't find an official page, so I don't know who looks after it or whether going in is allowed. It's easy to miss, so go with someone who knows the way, like your friend did.
